papers.title: Rational polynomial solvability reduces to stratifiability of semilinear sets
papers.abstract: A semilinear set is stratifiable if it is a finite union of linear sets whose periods have at most two nonzero coordinates, with no two periods in one component connecting alternating pairs of coordinates. We give a computable many-one reduction from the existence of a rational zero of an integer polynomial to deciding stratifiability. After the classical reduction to quadratic systems, we reduce rational solvability of these systems to a problem we call finite separation by Cartesian products of rational linear forms. Its input consists of rational subspaces $D_1,\ldots,D_k\le\mathbb Q^r\times\mathbb Q^r$. A separator is a map $(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\mapsto(u(\boldsymbol x),v(\boldsymbol y))$, where $u,v\colon\mathbb Q^r\to\mathbb Q$ are nonzero rational linear forms. The problem asks whether finitely many separators suffice so that every pair outside $\bigcup_iD_i$ receives, from some separator, a value attained at no pair in that union. We then reduce this problem to stratifiability. Ginsburg and Spanier's characterization of letter-bounded context-free languages} also induces a reduction from rational polynomial solvability to context-freeness of letter-bounded languages specified by semilinear exponent sets. An OpenAI preprint claims undecidability of rational polynomial solvability; if correct, our result settles the decidability of general stratifiability, a problem open since 1966.

papers.title: Noise-aware Verification and Synthesis of Quantum Programs
papers.abstract: This work provides a comprehensive framework for noise-aware quantum program analysis, ranging from logical foundations to model checking and automated synthesis. While most research on quantum programming considers an idealized, noise-free semantics for quantum programs, we reason about quantum programs that are executed on real, noisy hardware. We use the error models published by quantum-hardware vendors to give a hardware-dependent semantics to quantum programs. We then present a noise-aware quantum Hoare logic with a relatively complete proof system. We finally use state-space exploration techniques for the hardware-aware verification and synthesis of loop-free quantum programs. In this way, we synthesize optimal, hardware-dependent solutions for parity bit-flip, GHZ state preparation, and other problems that commonly occur as subroutines in larger quantum algorithms. We evaluate our method on all 55 hardware specifications provided by the IBM Qiskit toolkit. Finally, we also show that classical probabilistic branching is needed for optimality in quantum programming.

papers.title: An Ordinal Extension Characterization of the Regular Languages with Applications
papers.abstract: Given a language $A$ and a positive integer $j$, a $j^{\text{th}}$ $A$-extension is a string $y$ for which there exists a string $x$ such that $y$ is the $j^{\text{th}}$ string satisfying $xy \in A$. In this paper we show that ordinal extensions ($j^{\text{th}}$ $A$-extensions for various $A$ and $j$) constitute a subtle, but remarkably useful concept. We characterize the regular languages in terms of ordinal extensions, and we extract from this characterization two general methods for giving very easy proofs of nonregularity.
